prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth strip separates the enclosing rock walls from the open sky and shows that the left-hand rock surface is very near in frame 1, while the people in frames 2–5 stand at several depth layers along the canyon floor. In frame 2, the large person left of centre is roughly 1–2 m ahead, with a cluster about 2–6 m farther right; in frame 3, people range from about 1–3 m in the foreground to roughly 5–10 m down the passage, and a person partly cut off at the right edge is within about 1 m. Frame 4 places the two large, partly cropped foreground people within roughly 0.5–1 m and shows the remaining group several metres behind them; by frame 5 those close occluders have left the view, exposing a person near the wall at about 1–2 m and others roughly 3–10 m away. These near-to-far layers and occlusions are clearer than in RGB, but the map is monocular and uncalibrated, smooths people into nearby surfaces, gives no dependable inter-person metre measurements, and sometimes produces implausibly uniform silhouettes.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance masks isolate many people that overlap the similarly coloured rock in RGB: none are clearly segmented in frame 1, while frames 2–5 contain foreground figures plus a line of smaller people extending deeper into the scene. Mask size suggests people roughly 1–2 m from the camera in the foreground and about 3–10 m away in the smaller background group; adjacent background people appear within roughly 0.5–2 m of one another, whereas exact depth cannot be obtained from this map. The masks make left/right ordering and occlusion explicit—for example, the large figures in frame 4 block much of the group behind them, and several people are clipped by the top, left, or right image boundaries—but they do not reliably reveal front-versus-back orientation or whether faces look toward the camera. Across the frames, different large masks enter and leave the foreground as the viewpoint turns, while the distant group remains ahead; the isolated “ski” label in frame 3 and fragmented or merged small-person masks appear unreliable, and most rock, ground, helmets, ropes, and other gear are not identified.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only one standing person in frame 2, left of centre and roughly 1–2 m in front of the camera, with the head above the torso, legs separated below, and one arm bent or raised toward the left side. The skeleton provides limb configuration and joint-relative above/below and left/right positions that are harder to read against the rock in RGB, but it does not establish a reliable gaze direction; the head and torso arrangement suggests an oblique or partly turned body rather than an unambiguous front-facing orientation. No separate hand skeleton is visible, and the detected hands are not shown close enough to the camera wearer to establish arm’s-reach contact; only the person’s own adjacent upper body and gear would plausibly be within that person’s reach. Because every other visible person is missed in all five frames—including the very large foreground figures in frames 3–4—the pose map is highly incomplete and cannot support group distances, occlusion tracking, or approach-and-retreat estimates beyond this single detection.
